title: Over the sea horizon
question: Will raising your eyes recover a ship hidden below the horizon?
explanation: The eye height changes the tangent to a spherical sea. The lowest visible part of a distant ship therefore changes. A flat model does not hide the hull.
limits: Geometric horizon on a smooth spherical Earth; no atmospheric refraction. Curvature is magnified in the 3D overview.

title: A sphere and a disc cast shadows
question: If a disc turns edge-on to the light, does its shadow stay circular?
explanation: Parallel projection preserves a sphere’s circular outline in every orientation. A disc’s projection narrows to a line as it turns edge-on.
limits: Parallel geometric projection of an opaque sphere and thin circular disc. No diffraction or extended light source.

title: Precise can still be wrong
question: If five readings agree, must their average be correct?
explanation: Scatter measures repeatability; an offset shifts every reading together. Compare both with the marked reference length.
limits: Five deterministic illustrative readings, not a statistical confidence interval. The reference is assumed known.

title: Length, area and volume
question: A cube becomes twice as wide. How do its face area and volume change?
explanation: Count the unit lengths, squares and cubes: scaling multiplies length by s, area by s² and volume by s³.
limits: Dimensionless unit cubes; the logarithmic Powers of Ten explorer remains the authority for physical sizes.

title: A shallow layer over a city
question: Can ankle-deep rain add up to millions of tonnes of water?
explanation: Volume is footprint area times rainfall depth. One cubic metre of fresh water has about one tonne of mass.
limits: A rectangular, illustrative city footprint; no drainage, infiltration or forecast. The rain depth in the overview is enormously enlarged.

title: Two shadows measure a world
question: Why can two parallel sunbeams make different stick shadows?
explanation: Local verticals point in different directions on a sphere. The shadow angle equals the central angle in this two-city meridian model.
limits: Parallel rays, cities on one meridian, spherical Earth. Stadion length remains an explicit assumption.

title: One bounce, two observers
question: Does the ball travel vertically or along an arc?
explanation: Subtract the chosen observer’s position from every event. Changing frame changes the drawn path, not which events occur together.
limits: Steady nonrelativistic motion; identical ideal bounces. Train and ball sizes are schematic; distances are metres.

title: Three trains, one clock
question: Which train is really going backwards?
explanation: A velocity is always measured relative to an observer. The 70 km/h train passes the 60 km/h train at 10 km/h; the opposite train passes at 120 km/h.
limits: Illustrative constant speeds, no timetable data; carriage sizes enlarged.

title: A graph is not a road
question: After an out-and-back walk, can average velocity be zero while average speed is positive?
explanation: Distance adds every segment travelled. Displacement compares only start and finish. The slope of position against time gives velocity. On the smooth-motion preset, reduce the secant interval to approach instantaneous velocity.
limits: Piecewise ideal walking velocities change instantaneously at the marked times; a real walker takes time to turn.

title: Negative need not mean slowing
question: Can a negative acceleration make something go faster?
explanation: Compare velocity and acceleration directions. The same direction increases speed; opposite directions decrease it, regardless of coordinate signs.
limits: One-dimensional constant acceleration; arrows for different quantities use separate labelled scales.

title: Equal beats, unequal gaps
question: Does twice the elapsed time mean twice the distance?
explanation: Constant acceleration gives distances proportional to t². A rolling solid sphere has smaller acceleration than a frictionless sliding particle because some energy becomes rotation.
limits: Uniform solid sphere rolls without slipping; slider is an ideal particle. No rolling resistance. Markers are equal-time samples.

title: Stop exactly at the top
question: At the highest point, which graph reaches zero?
explanation: The height has a maximum while velocity passes through zero. Acceleration remains −9.8 m/s² throughout the ideal flight.
limits: No air. The horizontal graph axis is time; it is not a horizontal flight direction.

title: After the hand lets go
question: What happens when friction approaches zero?
explanation: After release there is no forward hand force. A backward contact force changes velocity; when it is removed, the same velocity continues.
limits: A 1 kg book is pushed for 0.40 s to a selected release speed, then slides with constant kinetic friction and no air. Hand departure is visible; replay restarts after five seconds.

title: What pushes an arrow after release?
question: Once the string leaves the arrow, what supplies a forward force?
explanation: The bow supplied a contact force before release. After release gravity and air drag change the arrow’s velocity; no stored forward force is needed to keep it moving.
limits: Point-particle flight with linear drag, no lift or wind; the arrow is aligned with velocity. Body size is enlarged; no quantitative archery prediction.

title: Who pushed the passenger?
question: From the platform, what slows first when the train brakes?
explanation: The floor slows the passenger’s feet. An initially unrestrained upper-body marker keeps its old motion, so it advances relative to the braking carriage.
limits: Short-time rigid hinged-torso model with floor-driven feet and no muscle response or stepping. A separate loose bag slides on an ideal frictionless floor; no injury prediction. Coordinates transform using the same train clock.

title: At the contact
question: Does friction always equal its maximum value?
explanation: Static friction matches the applied force up to a limit. Once sliding begins, deforming and breaking contact junctions resist relative sliding.
limits: Schematic contact junctions; constant coefficients μs=0.50 and μk=0.35. Real contacts also involve adhesion and deformation.

title: A short push on a plate
question: Will doubling the plate’s mass stop it moving?
explanation: Friction grows with mass, but so does inertia. Pull duration controls the impulse and the resulting displacement; mass cancels in this ideal model.
limits: Constant sliding friction μ=0.30 on both cloth and bare table, no hem or tipping. This is a virtual experiment.

title: Pulls at an angle
question: Do two 5 N pulls always add up to 10 N?
explanation: Add vectors head to tail. The resultant depends on their directions; acceleration is the resultant divided by mass.
limits: Point-mass cart on a frictionless horizontal surface; force and acceleration scales differ.

title: Change the force; change the mass
question: If the same resultant acts on twice the mass, how does its acceleration change?
explanation: Add vectors head to tail. The resultant depends on their directions; acceleration is the resultant divided by mass.
limits: Point-mass cart on a frictionless horizontal surface; force and acceleration scales differ.

title: A table is a very stiff spring
question: If a tabletop hardly moves, how can it push?
explanation: A small deformation produces a restoring force. Stiffer supports need less deformation for the same force. On a slope, the normal balances the perpendicular part of weight. The table preset exposes schematic material sites whose small relative displacements are enlarged.
limits: Hooke-law support analogies; all deformation magnified. On the inclined support, separate static friction balances the downhill component.

title: One interaction, two objects
question: Can equal opposite forces give very different accelerations?
explanation: An interaction gives equal and opposite forces on two different objects. Their accelerations differ inversely with their masses. Selecting one object leaves its own force visible. The standing-person preset separates the two balanced forces on the person from their partners on Earth and floor.
limits: Two isolated bodies with a prescribed mutual force for a short instant; not a collision damage model.

title: Throw something, move yourself
question: What can an astronaut push on in empty space?
explanation: The astronaut and thrown object receive equal and opposite momentum. Repeated ejections use the same two-body accounting; there is no external air.
limits: Discrete ideal ejections, no gravity or drag; exhaust icons are parcels of finite mass, not literal molecules.

title: Air and gravity are separate controls
question: Would a feather fall slowly on the Moon because there is no air?
explanation: Gravity sets the initial acceleration. Drag grows with speed, shape and air density. Removing air restores equal acceleration regardless of mass.
limits: Vertical quadratic drag with assumed effective drag areas; fixed g, no tumbling, wind or changing atmosphere.

title: Drop from a moving car
question: Where does the ball land relative to the car?
explanation: The released ball retains the car’s horizontal velocity. It falls vertically in the car frame and along a parabola in the ground frame.
limits: Level constant-speed car; no air or rotation. Start height 0.75 m.

title: Turning a velocity arrow
question: How can speed stay constant while velocity changes?
explanation: Equal-length velocity arrows turn. Their vector difference points towards the centre. Releasing the constraint continues along the tangent.
limits: Planar circle of radius 2 m; release removes only the inward constraint. Floor view neglects vertical motion.

title: The apple, the Moon and a shared centre
question: Does the Moon move around an Earth that is perfectly fixed?
explanation: The two bodies orbit a common centre of mass. A separate comparison shows the inverse-square change in gravitational acceleration. The apple/Moon preset compares 4.90 m in one second with the gap below a lunar tangent in one minute.
limits: Circular two-body teaching orbit; Earth/Moon sizes and orbital separation enlarged independently for visibility. No tidal or solar perturbations.

title: A falling room and a relaxed spring
question: Does a zero accelerometer reading mean zero gravity?
explanation: A freely falling room and astronaut have the same gravitational acceleration. With no support force, the spring-mass sensor relaxes even though gravity remains strong.
limits: Ideal local free fall, ignoring gravity gradients and station rotation. Sensor is a spring analogy; no device is connected.

title: Kepler’s equal-time sweeps
question: Does a planet cover equal distances in equal times?
explanation: For equal amounts of time, the line joining the planet to the central body sweeps equal areas. The planet moves faster near the central body. Bigger orbits take longer: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.
limits: Two-body Newtonian ellipses; normalized units with GM=1. Eccentricity is user-selected, not necessarily a real planet.

title: A tiny pull twists a wire
question: What changes when the large lead balls switch sides?
explanation: Both gravitational torques change sign. The wire twists until its restoring torque matches the tiny gravitational torque.
limits: Assumed small-angle apparatus; includes attraction of both large balls on both small ones. The displayed twist is enormously enlarged. Not a reconstruction of Cavendish’s measured trace.

title: A small nudge leaves a message
question: Does adding one small planet leave the same predicted orbit?
explanation: Compare the two-body path with a restricted three-body calculation. The separate residual view reveals the small difference that is hard to see on the main orbit.
limits: Illustrative planet mass and prescribed circular orbit; not historical Neptune or Halley data. Heliocentric indirect acceleration is included.

title: Burn here, change the far side
question: Does a forward burn at perigee push the spacecraft radially outwards?
explanation: An impulse along the path immediately changes velocity; the larger apogee appears later. A retrograde lunar flyby burn can change positive orbital energy to a bound orbit.
limits: Educational impulsive two-body burns, separate Earth and Moon panels. The original mission explorer retains the published ISRO orbit sequence; this is not a flight trajectory reconstruction.

title: Pressure has no preferred direction
question: What changes when the same load is turned onto a smaller face?
explanation: Force stays fixed while force per area changes. In the immersed mode, forces are perpendicular to every face and pressure increases with depth.
limits: Uniform fresh-water density; rectangular body. Contact and immersed views use different arrow scales. Within the immersed view, equal-area face arrows share one gauge-pressure scale; values are printed. The immersed cube is held while pressure forces are measured; the arrows are not a complete free-body diagram. The solid has fixed 0.20 × 0.10 × 0.05 m dimensions and is turned onto one of three faces.

title: The outside air does the pushing
question: Can an empty space pull water up a tube?
explanation: A pressure difference supports a liquid column. Change the gas pressure at the top, the liquid density or the apparatus to see the same balance.
limits: Static columns, negligible liquid vapour pressure and capillary forces. Hemispheres use projected circular area; no hazardous apparatus is proposed. The glass inset is enlarged and shows initial forces only, not subsequent water flow.

title: Same depth, same pressure
question: Does a wide lake make more pressure than a narrow tube at the same depth?
explanation: Pressure at a point depends on depth, density and surface pressure. A dam’s total force adds a triangular distribution; a piston adds the same pressure everywhere.
limits: Static incompressible fresh water; vertical dam. Vessel shapes are illustrative and pressure probes are compared at equal depths.

title: The same steel, a larger hull
question: Can adding enclosed air change the steel’s weight?
explanation: The steel’s mass is fixed. A larger watertight envelope displaces more liquid before submerging. Cargo changes weight; salinity changes the displaced volume needed.
limits: Ideal rectangular watertight hull in calm liquid, with no stability or flooding model. The layered case uses an egg-shaped solid at a sharp density interface; no mixing, surface tension or real-egg variability.

title: Choose what you count
question: If the ball loses mechanical energy, must the total account fall?
explanation: Choose the ball alone, ball plus Earth, or the surroundings too. Thermal accounts reveal where the mechanical energy went; gravitational energy belongs to the ball–Earth interaction.
limits: Ideal flights and instantaneous lossy impacts; 64% mechanical-energy retention per bounce. Thermal allocations 30/40/30% are illustrative, sound counted after absorption.

title: Two ways to stop a moving ball
question: When speed doubles, what happens to stopping time and stopping distance?
explanation: At fixed resisting force, impulse determines stopping time and work determines stopping distance. Momentum doubles, kinetic energy quadruples.
limits: Constant resisting force; no universal claim about real flour or clay crater depths.

title: Different routes, the same rise
question: Does a longer ramp store more gravitational energy than a lift to the same floor?
explanation: Only the rise changes the gravitational store. A ramp needs less force along a longer route. A perpendicular support force does no mechanical work during a horizontal move.
limits: Quasistatic motion, no friction or physiological energy costs. Ramp/stairs geometry is schematic.

title: Power is the rate, energy is the amount
question: Which uses more energy: a 2 kW geyser for 15 minutes or a 10 W lamp all day?
explanation: Power is the slope of cumulative energy. Duration matters as well as the wattage. One kWh is 3.6 MJ.
limits: Constant label power; ignores appliance duty cycles and billing tariffs.

title: Follow the shaft and the energy
question: Where does the rest of a power station’s input go?
explanation: A turbine turns a generator while the account splits electrical output from rejected energy. A finite spinning wheel slows when a lamp draws energy from it.
limits: Illustrative adjustable efficiencies, no present-day Mumbai supply claim. Rotor kinematics are schematic; the energy account is exact for the stated model.

title: Stevin’s wreath of spheres
question: Why do four beads on a gentle slope balance two on a steep one?
explanation: For a uniform chain, mass on each slope grows with its length while the downhill fraction shrinks inversely with length. Both downhill forces equal linear density × g × height.
limits: Uniform flexible chain on frictionless slopes, symmetric hanging portion. Geometry follows the selected height; beads represent equal chain lengths.

title: A heat engine needs two temperatures
question: Could an engine turn all incoming heat into work?
explanation: The reversible limit depends on hot and cold absolute temperatures. Work plus rejected energy always equals input; real performance can lie below that limit.
limits: Ideal reservoir model and schematic piston; temperatures are kelvin, not Celsius. The reversible limit is not a claim of an actual engine’s efficiency.
